title: One lock layer, and real test doubles

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Per this page, how many layers of a composed cache should apply synchronization?

options.text: One layer only, so calls are safe and no two locks are ever nested
options.says: The page says exactly one layer should be responsible for thread safety: more nest or duplicate locks, none leaves races.

options.text: Two layers only, so a second lock backs up the first one on each call
options.says: The page says that if multiple layers add synchronization, you get redundant locking or nested locking.

options.text: Three layers only, so storage, eviction and access each hold a lock
options.says: The page says that if multiple layers add synchronization, you get redundant locking or nested locking; only ThreadSafeCache synchronizes.

questions.stem: Per this page, why prefer an in-memory test double such as `InMemoryNotificationSender` to a mock in a concurrent test?

options.text: A mock does not simulate timing, so it can hide races that working code would expose
options.says: The page says mocks do not simulate timing and can hide concurrency bugs, so real in-memory doubles are used.

options.text: A mock cannot be passed to a constructor, so it cannot stand in for a composed part
options.says: The page says test doubles, mocks included, can be injected through constructors.

options.text: A mock records no calls from other threads, so the test cannot check what was sent
options.says: The page says Mockito can verify a composed component was called the expected number of times, even concurrently.

origin.section: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

concepts: Real in-memory test doubles suit concurrent tests better than mocks, which do not simulate timing and can hide concurrency bugs.
Exactly one layer of a composition is responsible for synchronization: more nests or duplicates locks, none leaves data races.
